You are COVID Trials AI, a research assistant that answers questions about COVID-19 from a database of 10,269 ClinicalTrials.gov study records (1,096 with posted results) and 1,630 open-access papers that report those trials. People asking range from researchers and clinicians to members of the public.

How to answer:
- Base factual claims on what your tools return, and cite each one right after the claim with its ID in square brackets, like [NCT04381936] or [PMC9006771]. Cite only sources you retrieved in this conversation. If the database lacks good evidence, say so plainly instead of filling gaps from memory; brief general background is fine if you label it as such.
- Weigh the evidence. Large randomized controlled trials outweigh small, open-label or observational studies. Say what kind of study each finding comes from (design and size), and point out when studies disagree and why that might be.
- For exact numbers prefer posted registry results (get_trial); use papers for context and interpretation.
- When a question calls for statistics (pooling trials, risk ratios, rates, confidence intervals), compute them with code execution using numbers you retrieved. Run every calculation as code, even simple ones, rather than working it out in your head. Show the input numbers in a table, name the method and its assumptions, and say when trials are too different to combine. Watch for arms of the same trial that share a placebo group: pooling them counts those placebo patients twice.
- Write for the person asking: start with a short bottom line in plain language, then the details. Briefly define technical terms.
- This is research information, not medical advice. When a question is about someone's own care, say once, briefly, that decisions should be made with a clinician.
- Coverage: studies registered with COVID-19 as a condition, collected November 2026. Only papers linked from the registry are included, so some published trials are missing. Mention this when it limits an answer.
In the EPIC-HR Paxlovid trial, what was the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat to prevent one hospitalization or death?

[NCT04960202] EPIC-HR: Study of Oral PF-07321332/Ritonavir Compared With Placebo in Nonhospitalized High Risk Adults With COVID-19
Official title: AN INTERVENTIONAL EFFICACY AND SAFETY, PHASE 2/3, DOUBLE-BLIND, 2-ARM STUDY TO INVESTIGATE ORALLY ADMINISTERED PF-07321332/RITONAVIR COMPARED WITH PLACEBO IN NONHOSPITALIZED SYMPTOMATIC ADULT PARTICIPANTS WITH COVID-19 WHO ARE AT INCREASED RISK OF PROGRESSING TO SEVERE ILLNESS
INTERVENTIONAL | phase: PHASE2, PHASE3 | allocation: RANDOMIZED | masking: QUADRUPLE
Status: COMPLETED | start: 2021-07-16 | enrollment: 2091
Sponsor: Pfizer | linked open-access papers: none
Arm: PF-07321332/ritonavir (EXPERIMENTAL): Orally administered PF-07321332+ritonavir
Arm: Placebo (PLACEBO_COMPARATOR): Orally administered placebo

Posted results: 7 outcome measures matching the filter.

Primary outcome: Percentage of Participants With Covid-19 Related Hospitalization or Death From Any Cause Through Day 28- Modified Intent-To-Treat (mITT) Population
Time frame: From Day 1 to Day 28
Description: Percentage of participants with COVID-19 related hospitalization or death from any cause during the first 28 days of the study was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier (KM) method. Using KM method, survival probability for each time interval was calculated as the number of participants surviving divided by the number of participants at risk. Participants who had the event, dropped out, or moved out were not counted as "at risk" i.e., participants who were lost were considered "censored" and were not counted in the denominator.
Measure: NUMBER (95% Confidence Interval), unit: Percentage of participants
Participants analyzed: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 671; Placebo: 647
Result: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 0.752 (0.313 to 1.796); Placebo: 6.888 (5.172 to 9.146)
Analysis: Comparison of PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg, Placebo, Percentage difference = -6.137, 95% CI -8.208 to -4.066, p = <0.0001, method: Normal approximation

Secondary outcome: Number of Participants With Treatment Emergent Adverse Events (TEAEs)
Time frame: From start of study intervention (Day 1) up to end of safety follow-up (Day 34)
Description: An adverse event (AE) was any untoward medical occurrence in a participant, temporarily associated with the use of study intervention, whether or not considered related to the study intervention. Serious adverse event (SAE) was any untoward medical occurrence that, at any dose: resulted in death; required inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization; was life-threatening; resulted in persistent or significant disability/ incapacity; congenital anomaly/birth defect; a suspected transmission via a Pfizer product of an infectious agent, pathogenic or non-pathogenic and other important medical events. AEs included both SAEs and all non-SAEs. An AE was considered as TEAE if the event started on or after start date of study intervention.
Measure: COUNT_OF_PARTICIPANTS , unit: Participants
Participants analyzed: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 1038; Placebo: 1053
Result: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 228; Placebo: 256

Secondary outcome: Number of Participants With AEs Leading to Discontinuation and Serious Adverse Events (SAEs)
Time frame: From start of study intervention (Day 1) up to end of safety follow-up (Day 34)
Description: An AE was any untoward medical occurrence in a participant, temporarily associated with the use of study treatment, whether or not considered related to the study treatment. An SAE was any untoward medical occurrence that, at any dose: resulted in death; required inpatient hospitalization or prolongation of existing hospitalization; was life-threatening; resulted in persistent or significant disability/ incapacity; congenital anomaly/birth defect; a suspected transmission via a Pfizer product of an infectious agent, pathogenic or non-pathogenic and other important medical events.
Measure: COUNT_OF_PARTICIPANTS , unit: Participants
Participants analyzed: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 1038; Placebo: 1053
AEs leading to study discontinuation: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 0; Placebo: 13
SAEs: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 18; Placebo: 71

Secondary outcome: Percentage of Participants With Covid-19 Related Hospitalization or Death From Any Cause Through Day 28- Modified Intent-To-Treat 1 (mITT1) Population
Time frame: From Day 1 to Day 28
Description: Percentage of participants with COVID-19 related hospitalization or death from any cause during the first 28 days of the study was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method.
Measure: NUMBER (95% Confidence Interval), unit: Percentage of participants
Participants analyzed: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 977; Placebo: 989
Result: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 0.933 (0.487 to 1.786); Placebo: 6.571 (5.180 to 8.318)
Analysis: Comparison of PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg, Placebo, Percentage difference = -5.638, 95% CI -7.308 to -3.967, p = <0.0001, method: Normal approximation

Secondary outcome: Number of COVID-19 Related Medical Visits- mITT Population
Time frame: From Day 1 up to Day 34
Description: Medical visits included emergency room, practitioner's office, home healthcare services, urgent care, telephone consultation, outpatient infusion center, other, COVID-19-related-hospitalization (intensive care unit \[ICU\] and non-ICU stays). In this outcome measure, COVID-19-related medical visits of participants were reported.
Measure: NUMBER , unit: Visits
Participants analyzed: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 671; Placebo: 647
Result: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 22; Placebo: 81

Secondary outcome: Number of COVID-19 Related Medical Visits- mITT1 Population
Time frame: From Day 1 up to Day 34
Description: Medical visits included emergency room, practitioner's office, home healthcare services, urgent care, telephone consultation, outpatient infusion center, other, COVID-19-related-hospitalization (ICU and non-ICU stays). In this outcome measure, COVID-19-related medical visits of participants were reported.
Measure: NUMBER , unit: Visits
Participants analyzed: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 977; Placebo: 989
Result: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 40; Placebo: 128

Secondary outcome: Number of COVID-19 Related Medical Visits- mITT2 Population
Time frame: From Day 1 up to Day 34
Description: Medical visits included emergency room, practitioner's office, home healthcare services, urgent care, telephone consultation, outpatient infusion center, other, COVID-19-related-hospitalization (ICU and non-ICU stays). In this outcome measure, COVID-19-related medical visits of participants were reported.
Measure: NUMBER , unit: Visits
Participants analyzed: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 1038; Placebo: 1053
Result: PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: 45; Placebo: 144

Adverse events summary
PF-07321332 300 mg + Ritonavir 100 mg: serious 19/1038, other 234/1038, deaths 0/1038
Placebo: serious 72/1053, other 228/1053, deaths 15/1053
Most common serious events (participants affected, all groups): COVID-19 pneumonia (43); Pneumonia (12); COVID-19 (9); Acute respiratory failure (5); Dyspnoea (5); Pneumonitis (5); Creatinine renal clearance decreased (3); Hypoxia (2); Interstitial lung disease (2); Pulmonary embolism (2)

mITT (<=3d) ARR 6.137 NNT 16.3 NNT CI 12.2 - 24.6 RRR 89.1
mITT1 (<=5d) ARR 5.638 NNT 17.7 NNT CI 13.7 - 25.2 RRR 85.8

**Bottom line:** In EPIC-HR, nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) lowered the 28-day risk of COVID-19 hospitalization or death by about **6.1 percentage points**. That means about **16 high-risk patients needed treatment to prevent one hospitalization or death**.

**Source:** EPIC-HR [NCT04960202] was a large Phase 2/3 trial run by Pfizer. Patients were randomly assigned to the drug or a placebo (a dummy pill), and neither patients nor study staff knew who got which (double-blind). It enrolled 2,091 adults with COVID-19 who were not in hospital but were at high risk of getting severely ill. The figures below are the results Pfizer posted to ClinicalTrials.gov.

**Results**

The outcome is COVID-19-related hospitalization or death from any cause by day 28. The posted percentages are Kaplan-Meier estimates, a method that accounts for patients who left the study early. The registry reports the risk difference and its 95% confidence interval (CI, the range the true value likely falls in). I worked out the number needed to treat (NNT) from those numbers in code.

| Population | Paxlovid | Placebo | Absolute risk reduction (95% CI) | NNT (95% CI) | Relative risk reduction |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mITT, primary analysis (n=671 vs 647) | 0.75% | 6.89% | **6.14 points** (4.07–8.21), p<0.0001 | **~16** (12–25) | ~89% |
| mITT1, broader population (n=977 vs 989) | 0.93% | 6.57% | 5.64 points (3.97–7.31), p<0.0001 | ~18 (14–25) | ~86% |

- **Absolute risk reduction (ARR):** the placebo group's risk minus the treated group's risk.
- **NNT:** 100 ÷ ARR (in percentage points). The NNT range comes from flipping the ends of the ARR's confidence interval.

**Deaths and safety** (all 2,091 treated patients): 0 of 1,038 patients on Paxlovid died, compared with 15 of 1,053 on placebo. Serious adverse events (serious medical problems during the study, whatever the cause) were less common with Paxlovid: 19 vs 72 patients [NCT04960202].

**Things to keep in mind**
- The registry entry doesn't spell out how mITT and mITT1 differ. From general background, not from this database: the primary mITT analysis covered patients treated within 3 days of symptoms starting, and mITT1 extended this to 5 days. That fits the slightly smaller benefit seen in mITT1.
- An NNT only applies to people at a similar starting risk. Also from general background: EPIC-HR enrolled unvaccinated people during the Delta wave in 2021, when about 7% of the placebo group was hospitalized or died. Today most people are vaccinated or have had COVID, so the starting risk is usually lower. The relative benefit could be similar, but the absolute benefit would be smaller and the NNT larger. Later trials in standard-risk and vaccinated groups would help check this, but I didn't search for them here.
- No published paper on EPIC-HR is linked in this database, so these numbers come only from the registry results.
